title.narrative: ROAP/AFG02/24/The Project for the Improvement of Living Environment for Vulnerable People in Urban Areas

description.narrative: The takeover of government in Afghanistan by the Taliban in August 2021 triggered a dire humanitarian crisis in the country, leading to serious violations of human rights, poor governance, and a sharp decline in socioeconomic development. With an estimated 23.7 million people, more than half of Afghanistan’s population, in need of humanitarian assistance in 2024 and over 90% living in poverty, international aid has reached vulnerable populations across the country considering life-saving services, but poor residents in urban areas have been often left behind, resulting in increased urban vulnerability. Decision-makers frequently assume that poverty, vulnerability, and social exclusion are features of rural areas, not cities. This is, however, not the case. Urban populations are facing more financial barriers than people in rural areas, spending more income on meeting their needs, contributing to increasing urban poverty. In addition, rapid migration into urban areas has also been remarkable; Some macro-level analysis indicates that in 1950, only 1 out of every 20 Afghans lived in cities, but in 2022, 1 out of every 4 lived in cities, and by 2060, it is estimated that 1 out of every 2 – 50% of the total population – will live in cities (UN DESA, UN-Habitat, World Bank). While many Afghans are fleeing from frequent natural disasters, seeking better employment opportunities, and living environment, Afghanistan has been experiencing a massive increase in the arrival of Afghan returnees from Pakistan following a government decree in September 2023. In Kabul and Herat, the two most populous provinces in Afghanistan, rapid urbanization and a changing climate increases the urban poor’s vulnerability to hazards. A critical but often overlooked factor impacting urban life is the poor state of the country’s key infrastructure related to the provision of essential services. In Kabul and Herat, the essential infrastructure for ensuring basic living environment to protect human rights of vulnerable populations is insufficient, even quantitatively and qualitatively. The protracted humanitarian crisis has strained the public health system, with most facilities having poor infrastructure and limited capacity to provide healthcare services. Deteriorating buildings, outdated equipment, and power issues hinder operations for basic services. The inadequate hygiene and sanitation facilities including clean water sources and waste disposal systems not only hampers healthcare access but also plays a critical role in the spread of diseases. Infectious diseases are the consequence and catalyst of poor humanitarian conditions, including poor sanitation, water quality and quantity, malnutrition, reduced school attendance, poor health, and reduced income. Infrastructure for socially vulnerable populations, particularly women, is not well developed. Against this backdrop, the project aims to improve the living environment of the urban poor through rehabilitating essential community infrastructure in Kabul and Herat Provinces in a sustained and disaster-resilient manner. The target locations will be 20 Gozars in 10 most vulnerable Police Districts (PDs) of Kabul (PD 20, 21, 17, 14, 18, 19, 22, 16, 13, and 6) and 18 earthquake-affected villages of Zindajan District in Herat. The target population will be 100,818 in Kabul and 6,628 in Herat (107,446 in total). Outcome 1: Access to basic services and livelihoods is improved through the rehabilitation of sustained and disaster resilient community infrastructure. The project team will implement infrastructure subprojects, i.e., rehabilitation of public health facilities, WASH systems, and roads with roadside drainages, in coordination with communities and key national stakeholders as required. These subprojects are based on gender- and disaster risk-sensitive spatial plans by taking the “Build-Back-Better (BBB)” approach. In connection with the infrastructure component, the activities through community participation for increasing waged income will be conducted to support livelihoods of the urban poor. • Output 1-1. Rehabilitating and retrofitting public health facilities by incorporating the BBB approach (through community participation). • Output 1-2. Rehabilitating and retrofitting comprehensive WASH systems, including water supply networks and public toilets by incorporating the BBB approach (through community participation). • Output 1-3. Constructing paved roads with roadside drainages by incorporating the BBB approach (through community participation). Outcome 2: Target communities’ self-reliance and ownership is enhanced by establishing spatial plans and taking community actions with voluntary contributions. With an aim to improve self-reliance and the ownership of community infrastructure, the project will conduct a wide range of community-based activities, including a household survey and workshops for community action planning.
